(a) whether any separate authority ha s been constituted for conservation

(c) if not, how the need to conserve lakes, ponds etc. would be taken care

 (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
20 

[2 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
(a) to (c) A National River Conservation Authority exists under the 
Chairmanship of Prime Minister to fana lize the policy frame-work and oversee 
the implementation of conservation and management plans of rivers and lakes. 
A water Quality Assessment Authority has been constituted under the 
provisions of Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 in May 2001 with Secretary of 
the Ministry of Environment and Forests as Chairman, for water quality 
management of surface and ground water bodies. A National River Conservation 
Plan is under implementation for conservation and pollution abatement of 
polluted rivers. Under this Plan, conservation and pollution abatement works 
have been approved in 153 towns along the polluted stretches of 28 rivers in 17 
States. The estimated cost of these works is Rs. 3343 crore against which 
Central grants amounting to Rs. 1068 crore have been released so far. 
Conservation and management of rivers is one of the monitorable targets under 
the Tenth Plan. For conservation and management of lakes, National Lake 
Conservation Plan is under implementation. Under this scheme, plans for 
conservation and management of 7 urban polluted lakes have been approved 
at an estimated cost of Rs. 27.22 crore. These projects are under 
implementation and Central grants amounting to Rs. 9.79 crore have been 
released to the State Governments concerned so far.

Sariska Tiger Reserve from 1.2.2002 to  date. Important reasons of death 
include infighting injuries, traumma, liver disease, poaching; and road 
accidents. The exact reason of death in case of two animals could not be

consumption in the country; if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI BRAJ

Steel Policy to draw out the road map of the iron and steel industry in the 
context of second generation reforms, restructuring and globalization. A 
drafting Committee under the Chairmanship of Development Commissioner 
for Iron and Steel has been set up to prepare the Draft National Steel Policy. 
The Committee has prepared a first draft and the same is under examination in 
consultation with major steel producers and associations. 
(b) A proposal has been mooted to enact a legislation—"Buy India Act" to 
encourage growth and development of indigenous steel industry by giving 
preference to indigenous steel produc ers in Government procurement on the 
lines of "Buy American Act". 
(c) The annual growth rate of steel consumption has been below the 
expected level in the last couple of years. Therefore, there has been mismatch 
between demand and supply with supply exceeding demand in certain 
categories of products. However, this mismatch is temporary and Government is 
making efforts to see that the demand is strengthened. Steps taken by the 
Government to raise consumption level of steel in the country, include (i) 
constitution of a National Campaign Committee to promote steel consumption 
through development of markets especially in the rural areas, (ii) encouraging 
usage of steel in new applic ation areas such as grain storage systems, crash 
barriers in highways and express ways, (iii) providing financial support to R&D 
ventures in iron and steel sector to reduce production cost and (iv) organizing 
seminars for dissemination of knowledge on the use of steel, etc.

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF FOOD PROCESSING 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM):  (a) Food processing industries 
operate both in the organized and unorganized sectors. Most of the processed 
food items have been exempted from t he purview of licensing under the 
Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951. Given this position, 
information on the number of units and in vestment thereon is not maintained

total number of factories in the f ood and Beverage sector was 23,831 and the

industries on its own. The Ministry, however, provides financial assistance through 
its plan schemes for development of processed food sector, including setting 
up of food processing industries. Du ring the year 2001 -2002, financial 
assistance of Rs. 8.40 crores has been extended for 48 proposals for setting

besides those assisted in the North Eastern Region.

estimated at 211.32 MT, according to the latest estimates;

and would impact favourably the GDP and food security; and

development of infrastructure for storage and distribution is adequate, to 
prevent crores of rupees worth of grain wastage? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH) : (a) and (b) Yes,

(c) The Food Corporation of India (FCI ) is the main agency which provides 
the capacity for storage of foodgrains. Besides, constructing its own godowns, 
FCI also hire storage capacity from other sources such as the Central 
Warehousing Corporations (CWC), State Warehousing Corporations (SWCs), 
State Governments and Private Partie s. The storage capacity of CWC and 
SWCs is also utilised for storing other notified commodities like fertilisers, seeds,

agencies procuring on behalf of FCI or having decentralized procurement is of 
the order of 87 million tonnes.

handling, storage and transportation of foodgrains in the country, the 
Government have announced a National Policy on handling, storage and 
transportation of foodgrains. According to the National storage policy, 
integrated bulk handling, storage and tr ansportation facilities for a total 
capacity of 21 lakh tonnes for wheat are proposed to be created in producing 
and consuming areas through Private Sector participation on Build-Own-
Operate (BOO) basis. The Government have also recently launched Gramin 
Bhandaran Yojana, under a Central Sector Scheme on Construction of Rural 
Godowns. The scheme envisages new storage c apacity of 18.50 lakh tonnes

Decline in growth of soyabean in M.P. 
*298. SHRI KAILASH JOSHI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) what are the reasons for decline in growth of soyabean in Madhya 
Pradesh; 
(b) whether ICAR has taken up any study in this regard in general, and worm 
affected crop in particular; 
(c) if not, what are the reasons therefor; and 
(d) whether Government propose to study the matter in depth; if so, by when? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) Soyabean is 
relatively new crop to India. In 1985 the areas of soyabean was about 1.34 mha 
which increased to 6.3 mha in 1998. Madhya Pradesh is the leading State of 
India for soyabean cultivation covering about 4.5 mha annually. In the initial 
years the growth rate of area, pro duction and productivity was very high. 
However, the area of soyabean in Madhya Pr adesh is under the process of 
stabilization which ranged between 4.46 mha in 1997 to 4.47 mha in the year 
2000-01. The productivity which was 764kg/ha in 1985 has reached 1100 kg/ha in 
1999-2000 wl lich is a positive growth. However, there has been decline in 
production in the last two years becaus e of unfavourable growing conditions in 
the State of Madhya Pradesh. 
(b) Yes Sir, the National Research Centre on Soyabean, Indore and All India 
Coordinated Research Project on Soyabean under ICAR have taken up studies to 
find out the reasons for low productivity of soyabean in general and worm 
affected areas in particular. Since soyabean is grown as rainfed kharif crop, 
adverse weather conditions affect the cr op drastically. Among the major factors 
responsible for low productivity are tjon-availability of good quality seed, 
cultivation under rainfed conditions and slow adoption of improved production 
technologies. In certain areas the crop is also affected by endemic diseases like 
rust (Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra) and insect pests like tobacoo caterpillar 
(Rajasthan). However, ICAR has developed rust tolerant varieties and integrated 
pest management practices for the control of important pests of soyabean. 
(c) and (d) Question do not arise.

Ground water imbalance in Punjab 
1775. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased 
to state: 
† Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
52 

[2 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether the Ministry of Agriculture or any other agency has 
conducted a study in Punjab, which shows that the State is heading towards 
ecological disaster and may turn into desert; 
(b) if so, the salient features of the study report; and 
(c) the reasons for the fall in the water level in rural areas and the 
measures for correcting the ground water imbalance in the State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) An ICAR Fact Finding Committee 
submitted its Report in June, 1998 entitled "Decline in Crop Productivity in 
Haryana and Punjab: Myth or Reality?" The Committee was constituted by 
Hon'ble Agriculture Minister, Government of India to assess agricultural 
productivity issues in Punjab and Haryana. 
(b)The report highlighted that duri ng the Green Revolution period in 
seventies, inadequate attention was paid towards future demands of inputs, 
particularly of energy, water, fertilizers and pesticides. The effort apparently was 
towards maximization rather than optimization of resource inputs. Significant 
changes in cropping pattern also took place in the region. Now growth rate in 
productivity of rice and wheat show clearly a decline in some of the districts of 
Punjab. The important recommendations of the report include the following: 
1. Agriculture in the State of Punjab needs to be diversified through 
inclusion of dairy, poultry, horticulture, vegetables and similar other 
enterprises. 
2. Micro-level planning at the district and block level should be 
carried out to identify more suitable land use patterns. 
3. Research to develop new varieties of rice and wheat with higher yield 
potential should be strengthened. 
4. Farmers may be given incentive for introducing pulse crops and 
green manures for long term agricultural sustainability. 
5. For controlling salinity and waterlogging the saline water from the 
region needs to be disposed off to a safe disposal site. 
6. Pricing policy, for fertilizers, water and energy should have the long-
term sustainability dimension. 
53 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2002] 
(c) Rapid increase in the number of tubewells from 1.92 lakhs in 1970-71 
to 8.95 lakhs in 1996-97 has resulted in over-exploitation of ground water in 70 out 
of 118 blocks of the State leading to decline in ground water level. The 
imbalance in the use of ground wa ter can be ameliorated though pr oper 
distribution of available water resources in the State, appropriate" crop 
planning and timely sowing of rice crop, ground water recharge projects in the 
Kandiregion and other potential sites, harvesting of rain water in paddy fields and 
village tanks, efficient use of saline and poor quality water and rationalization of 
water and energy pricing.

Ban on Use of Endosulfan 
1807.  SHRI CO. POULOSE: 
SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that continuous use of Endosulfan pesticide, causes 
severe damage to living organisms in the surroundings areas; 
(b) whether any study has been conduc ted to ascertain its effect on 
environment and on human life: 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether many developed countries have banned/restricted the use of 
this pesticide. 
(e) whether Kerala Government has also requested to ban it; 
(f) if so, whether any ban/restriction has been imposed on its use in the 
country; and 
(g) if not, whether Government would consider to ban its use? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) The Registration Committee constituted 
under Section 5 of the Insecticides Ac t, 1968 registers pesticides for use on 
food crops in the country only after satisfying itself regarding data on chemistry, 
bioefficacy, residues of the pesticides and their safety to human health, animals 
and environment. If pesticides are used as per the guidelines prescribed by the 
Registration Committee and following good agricultural practices, they do not 
pose any hazards to human health. 
(b) and (c) The Expert Committees constituted by the Government of India 
in 1991 and 1998 to review the continued use or otherwise of Endosulfan 
recommended its continued use. In view of media reports 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2002] 
about the hazardous effects of Endosulfan,  Government of Kerala constituted 
an Expert Committee in 2001 under the Chairmanship of Dr. A. Achuthan. The 
Committee concluded as follows:— 
'There is no evidence to attribute these health problems directly to 
endosulfan pollution, but there is no evidence to completely deny it". 
The Committee also recommended the ban on aerial spraying of 
pesticides in all cashew plantations in Kasargod district of Kerala, pesticide holiday 
for five years in Peria Division of Plantation Corporation of Kerala and promotion of 
Integrated Pest Management. On the direction of National Human Rights 
Commission, a study has been conducted by the National Institute of 
Occupational Health (NIOH) of the Indian Council of Medical Research and 
higher prevalence of unusual diseases like mental retardation, congenital 
defects and abnormalities of re-productive system in children in the affected 
villages of Kasargod district of North Kerala has b een reported in their first 
report. 
(d) As per the consolidated list of products whose consumption and/ or sale 
have been banned, withdrawn, severely restricted or not approved by the 
Government (V Issue United Nations, New York—1994), the use of Endosulfan is 
banned/severely restricted in about 12 countries of the world viz. Belize, 
Canada, Dominica, Denmark, Finland, Hungary, Netherl ands, Norway, 
Philippines, Singapore, Venezuela, Yugoslavia. 
(e) to (g) No request has been received from Kerala Government to ban the 
use of endosulfan. Moreover, Governm ent of Kerala has banned the aerial 
spraying of Endosulfan on all crops in the State. Apart from this, there is no 
ban/restriction on the use of Endosul fan in the country presently. The 
Registration Committee constituted under Section (5) of the Insecticides Act, 
1968 has constituted an Expert Group to study the effects of use of endosulfan 
in this perspective and make recommendations regarding its continued 
use/restricted use or otherwise.

1834. SHRIMATI N.R DURGA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the country was suffering heavy losses due to massive soil 
erosion; and 
(b) if so, the measures proposed to  maintain a balance between nature 
and development, ensuring environment-friendly growth? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMEN T AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALLU): (a) and (b) Soil erosion takes place due to natural factors like 
unstable geological formations of mountains heavy rains, cloudburst and biotic 
factors like faulty land use practices, construction activities, inadequate tree 
cover etc. in the catchment areas of t he major river systems. It is a major 
problem on degraded hilly slopes and areas prone to floods. However, there is 
no alarming report that the country is suffering from an unusual and 
unprecedented situation of soil erosion. 
Checking soil erosion and denudation in  the catchment areas of rivers, 
lakes and reservoirs in the interest of soil and water conservation is one of the 
basic objectives of the National Forest  Policy, 1988. The measures taken to 
check soil erosion include forest protection activities and Joint Forest 
Management Programme, National Afforestation Programme for plantation on 
degraded forest land, watershed development and soil conservation works on 
agricultural land etc. 
Special legislative measures like the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 are 
also in place to maintain a balance between nature and development. This Act 
regulates diversion of forest lands for non-forestry purposes and also provides 
for compensatory afforestation on equivalent/more area of non-
forest/degraded forest land. 
All these measures help to maintain a balance between nature and 
development, ensuring environment-friendly growth.

Computer Literacy and Studies in Schools (CLASS) was initially launched as a 
Pilot Project in the year 1984-85. The project was subsequently modified to 
make it a Centrally Sponsored Schem e. With the increasing thrusts on 
Information Technology (IT) in educat ion, many State Governments have 
launched their own Computer Education Initiatives in schools.The Department 
of Secondary and Higher Education has launched the revised CLASS scheme 
during 2001-2002. As per the norms of  the revised CLASS scheme, grant-in-
aid is provided to State Govts./UTs on the basis of Computer Education Plan 
(CEP) submitted by them. The CEP indicates the steps already taken by the 
State/UTs and the assistance, which they now require.The CEPs are 
examined by the Project Monitoring & Evaluation Group (PM & EG) headed by 
Education Secy, and funds are allocated to the States/UTs on 
recommendations of PM & EG. Grant-in- aid is provided to only Govt, and 
Govt, aided schools. Union Govt, provides 75% of the total sanctioned 
amount, subject to a maximum limit of Rs. 5.00 lakhs per school. The balance 
25% is borne by the State Govt./UTs. The scheme also provides 25% of funds 
from MPLADS in addition or as an al ternative to State Govt, contribution. 
Besides, Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangthan (KVS) and Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti 
(NVS) would convert one school per State/UT into a SMART school. A grant of 
not more than Rs. 25 lakhs would be given per SMART school. KVS and NVS 
would be given funds at the rate of Rs. 15,000/- per neighbourhood school to 
impart computer literacy to not more than ten neighbourhood schools to cover 
10,000 such schools over 3 years. A Statement showing amount sanctioned 
and released during 2001 -2002 is inclosed {See below). 
The University Grants Commission has been assisting colleges for 
procuring Personal Computers since 1987.  The objective of the scheme is to 
create awareness among staff and stud ents about use of the computer in 
various activities like administration, finance, examination and research. 
Generally, the colleges which are not having computer facility are given 
priority. The UGC has also provided financial assistance to the colleges, which 
have already been assisted upto 1994-95 to upgrade the existing facility or to 
procure latest version of the computer (2nd time grant). Under these schemes 
the UGC has provided financial assistance to 3919 colleges on account of first 
time grant and 650 colleges have been covered under second time grant so 
far.

1849. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the basic norms binding recognition of educational 
institutions as "Deemed Universities'; 
(b) whether recognition has been given to Regional Engineering 
College, Surathkal, Karnataka as a "deemed University'; 
(c) whether the Karnataka Government has recommended a few 
educational institutions for grant of Deemed University status; and 
(d) if so, the Centre's response thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERM A]: (a) University 
Grants Commission has laid down the guidelines for considering proposal for 
declaring an institution as Deemed to be University under Section 3 of the UGC 
Act, 1956. These guidelines inter-alia provide that, an institution should 
generally be; 
(i) Engaged in teaching programmes and research in chosen fields of 
specialization which are innovative and very high academic standards 
at the Master's (or equivalent) and/or research levels. It should also 
have a greater interface with society through extra mural, extension and 
field action related programmes. 
(ii) Making in its ateas of specializ ation, distinct contribution to the 
objectives of the University educ ation system through innovative 
programmes and on being recognized a9 a university capable of further 
enriching the university system as well as strengthening teaching and 
research in the institution and particularly in its area of specialization. 
(iii) Competent to undertake application-oriented programmes in emerging 
areas which are relevant and useful to various development sectors 
and to the society in general. 
(iv) institutions should have the necessary viability and a management capable 
of contributing to the university ideals and traditions. 
130 

[2 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Ordinarily, institutions affiliated to universities and which are offering only 
conventional degree programmes leading  to BA/B.Com/B.Sc. or MA/ 
M.Com/M.Sc, will not be considered for grant of deemed to be university status. 
However, such institution which is al so offering innovath/e programmes, and 
which has adequate resources, might be considered for recognition as a 
university. Supplimentary assistance for Innovation may be considered by the 
UGC only in such exceptional cases. 
Institutions which are imparting routin e type of instruction to full-time 
students or offering training programmes for in-service personnel, unless of 
high quality, would, generally, not qualify for recognition. 
In selective cases, outstanding research institutions specializing in Social 
Sciences, Sciences and Technology can be considered for research degree and 
highly specialized programmes at the Master's level. 
In case the institution is offeri ng a degree/diploma, professional 
subject(s), the academic programme(s) should be recognized by the 
concerned statutory authority e.g. Alt fndia Council for Technical Education (AiCTE), 
Medical Council of India (MCI), Dental Council of India (DCI), Central Council of 
Homoeopathy (CCH), Indian Nursing Council (FNC) etc. before it applies for a 
deemed to be university status under Section 3 of the UGC Act. 
This shall, however, not apply to de-novo institutions in the emerging areas 
with the promise of excellence, not yet fulfilling the prescribed guidelines of the 
UGC whose case will be considered for a provisional status for a Deemed to 
be University. 
(b) Ministry of Human Resource Development has granted Deemed to be

(formerly known as Karnataka Regional Engineering College, Surathkal).

individual personality, fast changing social dynamics, home environment, inability 
of children to cope with the demands and expectations of family, peer pressure 
and a situation in which career opportunities are very limited in relation to 
mounting number of aspirants and examinations being a major determinant of 
career path. 
The Central Board of Secondary E ducation (CBSE) ha s already taken 
several steps to help the students to overcome their difficulties like: 
• Arranging for a stress free environment in schools 
• Deciding on Introduction of like skill education 
• Elimination of overall aggregation of marks to reduce unhelathy 
competition among students 
•  Introduction of comprehensive and continous school based 
evaluation 
132 

12 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
• Providing facility of compartment examination in two subjects in Class 
X and one subject in Class XII 
• Providing three chances of compartment examination for Class X and 
XII 
• Restructuring of questions in some of the important subjects such as 
Science and Mathematics. 
• Publication of sample question papers and making schemes to 
familiarize teachers and students about the nature of questions and 
question papers 
Similarly, the Council for the Indian School Certificate Examinations (CISCE) 
has introduced measures like flexibility in the choice of subjects at the Secondary 
level, internal assessment, continuous  involvement of schools/teachers in 
updating and revising the prescribed curriculum etc. to facilitate learning and 
reducing stress on students. 
The CBSE has also starte d telecounselling on vo luntary basis by the 
educationists, psychologists, psychiatrists and seasoned principals of the 
schools. It starts functioning before and during the examinations and also during 
declaration of results to mitigate and def use the sense of anxiety and stress 
among the students. For 2002 examinations, CBSE had started helpline from 
31 centres in and outside the country. 
Recognising the importance of counselling parents in the matter the CBSE 
has written to all CBSE affiliated schools for organising such c ounselling 
sessions. A copy of the circular dated 10.07.2002 issued by the CBSE to all its 
affiliated schools giving suggestions to reduce stress and anxiety of students has 
been sent by the Ministry of Human Resource Development to all 
States/Govts./State Boards of Secondary Education for their information and 
use.

Disinvestment in Railway PSUs 
1882. SHRI R. S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Railways are not in favour of disinvestment in Rail India 
Technical and Economic Services and Indian Railway Construction 
Corporation; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) what are the recommendations of disinvestment commission in regard 
to these PSUs; and 
(d) the reaction of the Railways thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) Ministry of Railways is not in favour of 
disinvestment in Rail India Technical and Economic Services (RITES) and 
Indian Railway Construction Croporation (IRCON International Ltd.) 
(b) RITES is a consultancy organization under the Ministry of 
Railways which carries out studies as required by the Indian Railways, clients 
railways abroad and other sectors. RITES also is in the business of export of 
rolling stock and inspection of materials procured by the railways. IRCON is 
in the field of construction of railway projects which are of specialized nature. 
The Ministry is not in favour of disinvestments of Rail India Technical and 
Economic Services Ltd. (RITES) and Indian Railway Construction 
Corporation (IRCON International Ltd.) for the following reasons: 
(i) IRCON and RITES being construction and consultancy 
organizations can keep only a smal l work force on permanent basis. 
In the existing scenario of stiff competition in the construction 
industry, both in domestic and international market, only companies 
which are lean with respect to their fixed cadre 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2002] 
can sustain their profits. Presently the skills for undertaking rail 
related consultancies are acquired by RITES thougn personnel on 
deputation from railways. After disinvestments it will not be possible 
to induct railwaymen into RITES: It will affect the competence of the 
organization to carry out rail related consultancy in India and abroad. 
(ii) Activities of RITES/1RCON abroad afford an opportunity to railway 
personnel to observe developments which benefit the railway 
officers on repatriation. 
(iif) Indian Railways have got surplus manufacturing capacity in 
production units for manufacture of locomotives and coaches. RITES 
and IRCON are the export arms of  Indian Railways for export of 
locomotives, coaches, etc. For export of locomotives and coaches, a 
close coordination between Railway Research, Design and Standards 
Organisation, Indian Railway manufacturing Units and RITES is 
required.The railway rolling stock requirement varies from country to 
country and Considerable design inputs and manufacturing effort is 
required in most cases, e.g. the Indian Railways in association with 
RITES and IRCON have developed locomotive suitable for 'Cape 
Gauge' which is prevalent in some African countries and Southeast 
Asian countries. 
(iv) RITES also carries Cut independent third party acceptance testing for 
components procured by the Indian Railways. If RITES were to be 
disinvested, Indian Railways would have to create a new 
organisation for this. 
(v) Many of the projects undertaken abroad for construction and for 
operation of railway system are given to the PSUs on the strength of 
Indian Railway backing, e.g. the Letter of Intent given by the Malaysian 
Government for construction of US$ 1.5 billion Ipoh-Padang Besar 
doubling project on single tender without going ftirougti the process 
of formal tendering is only on the strength of the backing of Mirtistry 
of Railways. Government of India. Similarly, the contracts for 
operation management of Railway System in Colombia and Zambia 
have been secured by RITES based on the Railway operating 
experience of Indian Railways. 
168 

[2 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) Disinvestment of IRCON International Ltd. is under examination 
by 
Disinvestment Commission, who have yet to make their recommendations. 
For Disinvestment in RITES. Commission has recommended that: 
(i) A minimum of 51% of the Government equity may be given to 
employees (both present and past) of RITES. Government may 
retain 25% of the equity. Balance equity may be distributed among 
reputed infrastructure consultancy organisation and infrastructure 
leasing and financing organisations after suitable pre-qualification; 
(ii) The Railways should have an agreement with RITES under which 
continuous induction of talented railway personnel would be 
guaranteed for a period of 5 years. In addition, the Disinvestments 
Commission has also suggested; 
(iii) RITES should develop consulta ncy expertise outside railway area 
with a view to increase non-railway consultancy business. 
(iv) Export of rolling stock handled by the RITES can be handled 
directly by the Railways. 
(v) Inspection work related to quality assurance of purchased-items 
presently entrusted to RITES may be handled by the Ministry of 
Railways. 
(d) Ministry of Railways have not agreed to the recommendations 
and suggestions of Disinvestment Commission for disinvestments of 
RITES assisted in question 'C above for the following reasons: 
(i) The present net worth of RITES is Rs. 158 crores and the share 
capital is Rs. 2 crores. For sale of 51% of shares to-employees,, the 
Government should be able to realize 51% of the net worth i.e. Rs. 
80 crore approximately. Thus the hundred rupee Share would have 
to be sold for approximately Rs. 7800/-. Also the expected annual 
dividend of Rs. 3 crores, would yield an average return of only 1.9% 
to the employees. To realize Rs. 80 crores through employees as 
recommended by the Disinvestment Commission, on the average 
investment of the present employees of RITES would be in the 
range of Rs. 3.5 lakhs per employee if all the present, employees opt 
for it. This may not be possible. 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2002] 
(ii) Deputation of railway personnel to RITES, after disinvestments, would not be 
possible unless the PSU character of RITES is retained. 
(iii) Disinvestment Commission's suggestion that RITES may develop 
expertise in non-railway business, after disinvestments, would defeat 
the very purpose for which RITES was initially set-up. Indian 
Railways' requirement of consultancy expertise in railway area, would 
get diluted and may not be available after sometime as availability of 
railway expertise in RITES dwindles. 
(iv) The export of rolling stock was delegated to RITES only because Indian 
Railways was unable to handle it directly through Government 
departmental setup. The recommendation if accepted would immediately 
effect export of Railway rolling stock and Indian Railways efforts to 
utilize spare capacity available in workshops. 
(v) The work of quality assurance for purchase items was hived off as a 
non-core activity to RITES as an independent third party. If Ministry of 
Railways were to carry out inspection work, they would need to create an 
organization for the same at a time when Indian Railways are making 
every effort to contain growth of manpower.

Unsafe rail lines 
†1899. SHRIMATISAVITA SHARDA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the rail lines all over the country are 
becoming quite unsafe;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) to (c) No, Sir. Repair and maintenance of 
Railway track is an on-going process. Maintenance works are carried out 
regularly depending upon the need. For ensuring safety of traffic, track is 
inspected regularly and corrective action taken promptly wherever required. Track 
renewals are also undertaken depending upon the need of renewal and 
availability of funds. The following further steps have been taken to improve 
the safety:

enhancement works which also covers track renewal.

being used. This gives superior track geometry.

Ultra Sonic Flaw Detectors have been procured. Self Propelled 
Ultrasonic Rail Testing Cars are being procured.

Iron Ore Mining by KIOCL in Western Ghats 
1906. MISS MABEL REBELLO: W ill the Minister of STEEL be 
pleased to state: 
(a) why Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Limited (KIOCL) had started 
mining iron ore in the Western Ghats; 
(b) whether it is a fact that area has low-grade iron ore deposits; 
(c) if so, the reasons for the mining the deposits when the country has 
rich iron ore, almost above 60% in other parts of the country; 
(d) how long iron ore mining would go on in Kudremukh area; and 
(e) how much deposits would be taken out from that area? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI 
BRAJ KISHORE TRIPATHY): (a) to (c) M/s Kudremukh Iron Ore 
Company Limited was established in April, 1976 in terms of an agreement 
between Govt, of India and Govt, of Iran, to mine iron ore deposits in the 
Kudremukh area of Western Ghats for the purpose of export of iron ore 
concentrates to National Iranian Steel Industries Company, Iran.The iron ore, 
mined from the deposits at Kudremukh has iron content of 37%-38%, which 
is benef iciated to produce iron ore concentrates of iron content 67-68%. 
(d) and (e) The commercial production of Kudremukh Iron Ore 
concentrate commenced in October, 1981. The weathered Ore reserves, 
where currently mining is carried out, are estimated to last for another 5-6 
years. The mineable Primary Ore rese rves are estimated to sustain an 
additional mine life of about 15 years.  In the present area of operations, 
geological reserves of 1174 million tonnes of Primary Ore comprising 
inferred reserves of 562 MT and indicative reserves of 612 MT are 
established.The theoretical mine rese rves are 247 MT. Besides, there are 
other deposits in the vicinity with probable reserves of 4000 million tonnes. 
Freight rate for steel 
1907. SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR: 
         SHRI RAJU PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether freight rates for steel-m aking raw materials and finished 
steel in India is exorbitantly high, compared to other countries; 
186 

[2 August, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether high freight rates of steel makes it uncompetitive; and 
(d) if so, what measures Government propose to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL 
(SHRIBRAJ KISHORE TRIPATHY): (a) and (b) The factors which determine 
freight rates are the distance travelled, tonnage carried, type of goods (whether 
perishable or non perishable), frequency of use of the freight carrier etc. The 
weightage given for different factors is not uniform in all the 
countries.Therefore, a comparison of freight rates of different countries may not 
yield a correct picture. 
(c) and (d) The market price of steel is determined by several factors such as 
cost of raw materials, power tariff, fuel charges, workers' pay, cost of funds, 
freight rates etc. These factors are dynamic and are determined by the 
interplay of market forces. No single factor can, therefore, be held responsible 
for the prevailing prices of steel or its upward/ downward trends.
